title: Effect Size
tagline: Statistical significance tells you something is real. Effect size tells you if it actually matters.
what_it_is: Effect size is a number that tells you how big a difference or relationship actually is — independent of sample size. A result can be statistically significant (very unlikely to be chance) but have a tiny effect size (barely makes a difference in practice). Effect size separates 'we can reliably detect this' from 'this is worth caring about.'
key_points: Statistical significance (p-value) tells you whether an effect is real. Effect size tells you how large it is.
With a big enough sample, even a meaningless difference will be statistically significant.
Cohen's d measures effect size for comparing two means. Small ≈ 0.2, Medium ≈ 0.5, Large ≈ 0.8.
Pearson's r (correlation) is itself an effect size — it's already standardised between −1 and +1.
Always report effect size alongside p-values. A p-value alone is not enough.
why_it_exists: The p-value has a dirty secret: it's heavily influenced by sample size. Give a test enough data and it will find any difference 'significant', even one so small it has zero practical meaning. Effect size was introduced to answer the question p-values can't: okay, but how much does this actually matter?
what_it_measures: Effect size measures the magnitude of a difference or relationship in standardised units — meaning it's not in dollars or kilograms or clicks, but in a unit that lets you compare across different studies and contexts. It answers: if there is an effect, how big is it relative to the natural variability in the data?
intuition: A painkiller trial with 100,000 participants finds that Drug A reduces pain scores by 0.3 points on a 100-point scale. p = 0.0001. Extremely significant. But the effect size is tiny — the average person would barely notice. Meanwhile, a small study of 40 people finds that a specific therapy reduces depression scores by 12 points on a 20-point scale. p = 0.04. Less significant. But the effect is enormous — people's lives are materially better. The p-value is about reliability. The effect size is about importance. You need both.

example.text: Two groups of students: Group A studies with background music, Group B studies in silence. Group A scores: mean = 72, SD = 10. Group B scores: mean = 75, SD = 10. Cohen's d = (75 − 72) / 10 = 0.3. With n = 1000 per group, p = 0.001 — highly significant. But d = 0.3 is a small effect. The 3-point difference is real, but it explains almost nothing about student performance.
example.interpretation: The test is so large it detects a 3-point difference with high confidence. But 3 points on an exam is not a meaningful pedagogical finding. Effect size catches what the p-value misses.

breakdown.means: the means of the two groups you're comparing
the pooled standard deviation — a combined measure of spread across both groups
the effect size — how many standard deviations apart the two group means are
small effect — real but hard to notice without careful measurement
medium effect — visible to a careful observer
large effect — obvious difference, clearly visible in the data

when_to_use: Whenever you report a hypothesis test result — always pair the p-value with an effect size
When comparing results across different studies — effect sizes are standardised, p-values are not
When deciding if a result is worth acting on — 'significant' doesn't mean 'important'
when_not_to_use: Cohen's benchmarks (small/medium/large) are rough guides, not laws. A 'small' effect in medicine might save thousands of lives. Context matters.
Don't use Cohen's d for proportions or non-continuous outcomes — use Cohen's h or odds ratios instead
common_mistakes: Reporting only p-values and calling a result 'highly significant' without mentioning the effect size — this is still extremely common in published research
Treating Cohen's thresholds as absolute — 0.2 is not 'unimportant' and 0.8 is not 'important'. Always interpret effect size relative to the domain.
Confusing a large sample size with a large effect — big samples inflate significance, not importance
notes: Cohen himself warned that his benchmarks were arbitrary conventions for when researchers had no other basis for comparison. They were never meant to be universal rules.
In machine learning, effect size thinking shows up in model evaluation — a 0.2% improvement in accuracy might be statistically significant but not worth the added complexity of the new model.
ds_usage: Effect size thinking is essential in A/B testing — companies set a 'minimum detectable effect' (MDE) before running an experiment, which is directly an effect size judgement. It also matters in feature selection: a feature might be significantly correlated with the target but have near-zero effect size — not worth including. In model comparison, use effect sizes to determine if a more complex model is genuinely better, or just marginally so.
